default.p.55cong_n4-t1-p1.vietnamese:
Currently, the after-school childcare program (Note 1) has 18 children and 2 teachers. In March, 5 children are expected to leave the program. The children wanted to hold a farewell party, so they decided to organize one. They plan to buy cakes on the day. Cakes cost 100 yen each when bought individually (Note 2), while a box of 8 costs 700 yen and a box of 6 costs 550 yen.

（Note 1）After-school childcare program: A place that looks after elementary school students after school.

（Note 2）Sold individually (bara): One item at a time; not included in a set or box. Separate items.

default.p.55cong_n4-t10-p1.vietnamese: At the supermarket near his home, there is a service card that awards 1 point for every 100 yen spent. Each point can be used as the equivalent of 1 yen. The 10 sets of office supplies you ordered for me have arrived, so I have received them. The section chief took 2 sets, and I took 1 set. I am keeping the rest. If you email me to tell me whom to give them to, I will deliver them for you. I look forward to hearing from you.

default.p.55cong_n4-t12-p1.vietnamese:
Nishi City Library Rules for Lending Materials

1. Dictionaries, newspapers, and the latest magazines must be read inside the library.

2. You may borrow up to 8 items (Note 1). The loan period is two weeks, and items may be returned to any library in Nishi City. If an item is overdue by one week or more, you will not be able to borrow new items.

3. If you lose or damage library materials (Note 2), you must pay compensation.

4. CDs, cassette tapes, records, DVDs, and similar items are fragile, so they must be returned at the service counter rather than in the return box. Please take note.

5. If materials are not available at Nishi City Library, we will borrow them from another library and lend them to you. Materials belonging to another library must be returned at the service counter.

(Note 1) 8 items: eight pieces

(Note 2) Materials: here, books, CDs, cassette tapes, records, DVDs, and similar items held by the library.

I received an email from my older sister.

Dear Uta,

I am at the tie counter now, buying a birthday present for Dad. I am keeping the money you brought with you, but the two of us cannot buy a nice tie with 5,000 yen. I would like to choose the one costing 8,000 yen in the picture I just sent. Would you pay half for me? If so, I will buy it and bring it home.

Midori

default.p.55cong_n4-t15-p1.vietnamese:
Dear Mr./Ms. Yamada,

I am sorry, but I have a high fever and would like to take the day off. I sincerely apologize, but Mr. Smith of Ali Corporation will arrive at Narita Airport at 1:00 p.m. on an AMA flight, so could you please arrange for someone who speaks English to pick him up? I would like that person to take him to the North Hotel. I have reserved a table at Hana Restaurant for 7:00 p.m., so please pick him up at the hotel at 6:30 and take him to Hana. The department manager said that, if possible, he would also like you, Mr./Ms. Yamada, to join them for dinner. Please ask the department manager about the details. Thank you very much for your assistance.

Kawamura

Train announcement

We sincerely apologize for disturbing passengers who are in a hurry, but because a car and a train were involved in a collision near Oyama Station ( ) this train will be temporarily stopped. We will make an announcement once preparations for departure are complete, so please wait a moment.

（Note 1）乗車: Boarding a train or other vehicle.

（Note 2）接触事故: Here, an accident caused by a car and a train colliding with each other.

（Note 3）発車: A train's departure.

（Note 4）少々: A little / a short while (少し).

Call for Volunteers

Time: Sunday, July 1, from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. You may leave at noon.

Location: Mori Square (the forest)

Activities: Help people with physical disabilities move around and play with them. Lunch boxes will be provided by us.

Eligibility: High-school students and older

Other: Volunteer insurance will be paid for by us.　　Minna Association

(Note 1) Disability: Here, this means being unable to move as one wishes.

(Note 2) Insurance: Here, this means money paid when something is damaged or someone is injured.

Dear Takashi,

You're home already. I am going to the hospital to see Grandma for a little while, so I think I will get home around 9 o'clock. After you finish your snack, please go to your swimming class. Before you go out, remember to bring the laundry inside. I have left dinner in the refrigerator, so heat it in the microwave and eat it. Please wait until I get home to prepare the bath. Do your homework first.

Mom

((Note)) 取り込む: here, it means bringing in laundry that has been hung outside to dry

default.p.55cong_n4-t20-p1.vietnamese:
Regarding factory tours in Kitaichi Town

Tour days: Every Saturday in November

Hours: 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Factories: 20 businesses

・Two-hour guided tour: Free of charge (note). Buses depart at 10:30 a.m. and 1:30 p.m. A guide will accompany you and provide explanations. Since the route passes through seven factories, it consists only of sightseeing.

・Self-guided tour: Maps are available at the station. Some factories can be reached on foot, while distant ones can be reached by bus. A one-day bus pass costs 500 yen and allows unlimited boarding and exiting, making it very convenient.

・At every factory, you can also try making various items for prices ranging from 500 to 1,000 yen.

((Note)) Free of charge: 0 yen

default.p.55cong_n4-t22-p1.vietnamese:
Thank you very much for always using the Southeast Railway Line. This train is an express bound for Minamigaoka. Please note that it stops only at Kitamae, Higashino, and Kiyokawa stations. The next stop is Kitamae. Passengers traveling to intermediate stations such as Nagasaki, Fuji, Umeda, Ogawa, or Oyama should use a local train, which stops at every station. Please wait three minutes until the train departs.

（Note 1）Maido: always

（Note 2）Express train: a train that runs faster than a local train

（Note 3）Train that stops at every station: a train that stops at all stations; a local train

（Note 4）Departure: the act of a train or bus leaving

It was sunny throughout this morning, but since Typhoon No. 21 is approaching from the south, clouds will probably gather from the afternoon onward. By late afternoon, there will be places in the mountains where it rains. Late at night, rain will begin in many areas, so you should take an umbrella when going out. (Note 2) 来店: visiting a store

(Note 3) まことに: truly

(Note 4) 迷子: here, a child who has become separated from a parent

default.p.55cong_n4-t26-p1.vietnamese:
In Japan, when people meet for the first time in a business setting, exchanging business cards (Note 1) is considered normal. However, it seems that countries where business cards are commonly used, such as South Korea and Japan, are actually rare (A). In some countries, business cards are hardly used at all; in others, only certain people use them. There are also countries where only people who work with foreign clients have business cards. Moreover, some people do things that Japanese people would never do, such as writing a note on the business card they have just received while standing right in front of the other person. However, etiquette differs from country to country, so even when customs differ from those in Japan, we should not get angry.

Business Card Etiquette

1. Hold out the business card with both hands so that the recipient can read it, while stating your company name and your own name.

2. The person in the lower position presents their card first to the person in the higher position. Normally, the older person or the person with the higher position in the company is considered superior, but someone from the client company is considered superior to someone from the other company.

3. When several people are exchanging business cards, the highest-ranking person among those presenting cards gives theirs first to the highest-ranking person on the receiving side.

4. When giving and receiving cards at the same time, use your right hand to present your own card and your left hand to receive the other person's card. The person in the lower position should hold out their card so that it is lower than the card of the person in the higher position.

5. When receiving a card, be careful not to hold the part where the person's name is written.

6. After receiving a business card, do not put it away immediately. Leave it on the table (B) while you continue the conversation.

(Note 1) Business card: A small piece of paper containing a person's name, company name, telephone number, and so on.

(Note 2) Exchange: To give something and receive something in return.

default.p.55cong_n4-t27-p1.outline.1.note: The culture of giving chocolate has changed since its early days and is completely different from Christianity, but it will continue because Japanese people enjoy festivals.
default.p.55cong_n4-t27-p1.outline.2.label: How Valentine's Day is celebrated in countries around the world

default.p.55cong_n4-t27-p1.outline.3.note: Explains the meanings of the terms: advertising (宣伝する), true-love chocolate (本命チョコ), obligatory chocolate (義理チョコ), and sharing chocolate (シェアチョコ).
default.p.55cong_n4-t27-p1.vietnamese:
Valentine’s Day is the reason chocolate sells best in February. It seems that confectionery companies were the ones who created the connection between Valentine’s Day and chocolate. They advertised that giving chocolate to men on that day would convey women’s romantic feelings. At the time, it was almost unheard of for women to take the initiative in expressing their feelings to men. Perhaps the idea that “So I am allowed to do this” resonated strongly with women’s feelings at the time. From then on, it gradually became common for women to give chocolate to men, but things are different today from how they were in the beginning. Valentine’s Day in Japan is completely different from the Christian Valentine’s holiday, but because it suits Japanese people, who love festivals, I think it will continue to exist far into the future.

The way people enjoy Valentine’s Day differs from country to country. In Japan, honmei chocolate and giri chocolate are gradually declining, while more women are buying chocolate for themselves or sharing chocolate with friends. I hear that nothing is done in Muslim countries, but in Denmark, friends and romantic partners give one another a beautiful white flower called the snowdrop. In addition, men are said to send anonymous letters containing the symbol “..”; if a woman guesses who sent the letter, she receives a gift at Easter. In the Philippines, many weddings are held on that day. This is because the city government provides venues, flowers, and wedding cakes for them. It seems that many people are enjoying Valentine’s Day in their own ways, in ways that suit them.

(Note 1) Promotion/advertising: announcing something widely

(Note 2) Honmei choco: chocolate given to someone one truly loves

(Note 3) Giri choco: chocolate given to people such as coworkers who regularly help and support one

default.p.55cong_n4-t28-p1.vietnamese:
The first time I saw a meteor was in the village of Tekapo, New Zealand. The village made itself darker by lowering the streetlights and attaching shades over them so that the stars could be seen clearly. When I climbed the mountain and looked down, there was almost no light, and the sky was very dark. That was why I could see so many stars from the mountain. Among the countless stars, meteors streaked across the sky and fell. Everyone was delighted to have been able to watch the meteors. Today, Tekapo’s starry sky is said to be the most beautiful in the world and has become famous. Because it is so famous, many people have begun visiting Tekapo to look at the stars. Not long ago, hardly any tourists visited Tekapo, a village that seemed to have nothing except its starry sky. The person who discovered the extraordinary beauty of Tekapo’s stars was Japanese. At first, even when this person said, “Let’s make the village’s starry sky a World Heritage Site. We can make it a World Heritage Site,” none of the villagers believed them. Because it was the same starry sky they saw every day, the villagers had failed to recognize its extraordinary beauty.

There are also places in Japan that attract many visitors by making their starry skies a special attraction. I hear that these places were once remote areas, like Tekapo, with nothing special to see except the starry sky. Surely everywhere has things or places that seem perfectly ordinary to the people who live there but wonderful to outsiders. If such an attraction does not already exist, all they need to do is create something strongly characteristic of their village. If they can make use of it, they can create jobs—and perhaps save villages that seem likely to disappear.

(Note 1) Electric light: an appliance that uses electricity to illuminate the surrounding area

(Note 2) World Heritage Site: something precious to people around the world selected by UNESCO

(Note 3) Save: to help someone escape from dangers or difficulties

default.p.55cong_n4-t29-p1.vietnamese:
It is said that since around 2000, more and more people have come to think that having a name unlike everyone else's is a good thing, and unusual names, bizarre names, and names whose gender cannot be determined have also increased. Today, there are so many children with unusual names—about one in three—that teachers often cannot read them and face many difficulties. The kanji that may be used in names are regulated, but because some people read kanji however they like, unusual "kirakira names" have appeared. Some children even have names such as 「Himeboshi (Kira)」, 「Pikachuu」, and 「Mitsuki」. As a result, among children with unusual names, some reportedly say that they do not want to tell people their names, feel embarrassed by them, or use a different name in everyday life. These children are troubled because they were given strange names. In a survey on unusual names, 23.8% approved of them, while 76.2% opposed them. Nevertheless, the number of parents who put their feelings and hopes into such names and end up giving them to their children has not decreased. In the past, all of Japan was caught up in a controversy over the name 「Akuma」. Someone planned to name their child Akuma. At the time, many people objected, saying, 「It would be too cruel to the child to name him Akuma.」 In the end, the government refused to register the name 「Akuma」, but people generally believe that names like that should not be given. In a country where the Japanese television drama 「Oshin」 became popular, the name 「Oshin」 was reportedly once fashionable, perhaps because people wanted their children to grow up strong like Oshin. Since a name is used by other people more often than by the person who bears it, it is difficult to say that names people cannot read are very good. Nevertheless, if an unusual name gives a pleasant impression or the child likes it, perhaps it is not such a serious problem.

(Note 1) Kirakira name: An extremely unusual name that is not normally found

(Note 2) Komeru: To put into, to invest or place one's feelings in

(Note 3) Akuma: Someone who brings evil to people or makes people do evil

default.p.55cong_n4-t30-p1.vietnamese:
The scramble crossing in Shibuya, Tokyo, is very famous, and many tourists come to take pictures and try crossing it. A scramble crossing is an intersection where all cars are stopped at the same time, allowing pedestrians to walk in any direction they choose. There are about 300 such intersections in Japan, but Shibuya is said to be the only one where so many people cross at once. During the 7 seconds when the signal is green, about 3,000 people cross at the busiest time, yet everyone walks very skillfully. Tourists find this fascinating and come to watch. On rainy days, the umbrellas of many different colors moving across the intersection are said to look beautiful as well. There is probably nowhere else quite like this.

In addition, on December 31, known as Ōmisoka (New Year’s Eve), as well as on Halloween and when World Cup soccer matches are being held, many young people gather here. Although no event is organized, people seem to feel that it will be fun and continue to come and congregate. Some drink alcohol, while others shout loudly. The police warn them, “Because it is dangerous, please do not gather beside the intersection,” but they still refuse to leave. When large numbers of people gather in one place, no one knows what might happen. Since vehicles also pass through the intersection, it is even more dangerous. As a result, the police are always worried that an accident might occur. Therefore, on New Year’s Eve in 2016, they decided to prohibit cars from passing through this scramble crossing. This prevented traffic accidents, but many people reportedly still caused trouble as usual.

default.p.55cong_n4-t31-p1.vietnamese:
Water is made up of hydrogen (Note 1) and oxygen (Note 2), so it can be produced from air. However, in the past, almost no one thought that a machine like this would actually be needed or that water could be produced from air. Today, machines can produce water from air at home, but they do not produce much water, and the cost of producing it is high.

However, a machine developed in 2018 can produce 2,000 liters of water per day at a cost of only about 2 cents per liter. This is because the machine operates by burning wood and other materials, so it does not require electricity. Although issues remain, such as the machine’s high price, it will surely be useful because so many people are suffering from water shortages. However, we must not forget that the amount of water produced by this machine is only enough for drinking; it cannot yet produce enough water to grow rice or vegetables.

As the population increases, water is becoming increasingly scarce. There is a great deal of water on Earth (Note 4), but 97% of it is seawater, which cannot be used as it is. Of the remaining 3%, water sources such as glaciers (Note 5) and groundwater are also difficult to use. The water that people can easily use amounts to only about 0.01% of the water in rivers and lakes.

It is said that 663 million people (Note 6) around the world do not have clean drinking water, and that 300,000 children die each year because of contaminated water. Japanese people seem to use as much as 300 liters of water per day, but I think that even if there is a great deal of water, they are using it excessively and wastefully. Perhaps Japan, too, will eventually face water shortages. I think we need to use water more carefully and conserve it.

(Note 1) Hydrogen: H

(Note 2) Oxygen: O

(Note 3) Burn: To set fire to something

(Note 4) Earth: The planet where we live

(Note 5) Glacier: A large mass of ice resembling a mountain

(Note 6) 663 million people: 663,000,000 people

default.p.55cong_n4-t32-p1.outline.0.note: State that Japanese people take fewer annual holidays than Europeans and emphasize the need for rest to generate new ideas.
default.p.55cong_n4-t32-p1.outline.1.label: The policy of increasing long holidays and its positive aspects
default.p.55cong_n4-t32-p1.outline.1.note: The government increased the number of public holidays and moved holidays to Mondays (Happy Monday) to create consecutive breaks, benefiting the tourism industry.
default.p.55cong_n4-t32-p1.outline.2.label: Problems caused by adding more Mondays as holidays
default.p.55cong_n4-t32-p1.outline.2.note: The negative effects of concentrating holidays on Mondays: students receive fewer class periods, and prolonged hospital closures make emergency care difficult.
default.p.55cong_n4-t32-p1.outline.3.label: The author’s viewpoint and solution

default.p.55cong_n4-t32-p1.outline.4.label: Vocabulary notes in the passage
default.p.55cong_n4-t32-p1.outline.4.note: Explains key terms from the passage: public holiday (祝日), annual leave (年休), waste (むだ), and emergency hospital (救急病院).
default.p.55cong_n4-t32-p1.vietnamese:
Japan has 16 national holidays, more than many other countries. However, because few people take paid annual leave, the total number of days off in a year is actually quite small compared with European countries where people may take an entire month off. For this reason, some people worry: 「If people do not rest, new ideas will not emerge, and if Japan remains as it is now, it will have no future」. People also say: 「Taking time off work is not a waste. Ideas emerge while we are resting」. Therefore, it will become necessary to rest more in the future.

The government is also trying to give people more days off by adding national holidays or making the Monday after a holiday that falls on a Sunday a substitute holiday. In addition, four national holidays that were previously fixed on specific dates have been moved to the second or third Monday of the month. This is how the government is trying to increase the number of consecutive days people can take off. As a result, travel agencies and hotels are delighted when the number of travelers increases. However, because there are more Mondays off, schools lose a considerable number of Monday classes each year. In addition, when hospitals are closed from Saturday afternoon until Tuesday morning, people who become ill or injured during that period are forced to go to emergency hospitals. On holidays, even emergency hospitals have fewer doctors, so patients are sometimes not treated in time.

When it comes to holidays, which are essentially a personal matter, there is little the government can do. Companies, workers themselves, and society as a whole need to change so that taking time off becomes easier. To achieve this, I think people need to understand the importance of rest more clearly.

(Note 1) National holiday: A day off designated by the government to celebrate or commemorate something.

(Note 2) Paid annual leave: Leave that the government requires employers to provide to workers.

(Note 3) Waste/uselessness: Something that provides no benefit.

(Note 4) Emergency hospital: A hospital that is open when ordinary hospitals are closed.

default.p.55cong_n4-t33-p1.outline.3.label: Vocabulary notes in the passage

default.p.55cong_n4-t33-p1.vietnamese:
Rice is divided into three types. Eighty percent of the rice grown in the world is long-grain Indica rice. Countries such as Japan, South Korea, and the United States grow short, round Japonica rice. In addition, although it is produced in very small quantities, there is also large-grain Javanica rice, which is grown in Indonesia, Italy, and elsewhere. Foreigners often praise Japanese rice as delicious. However, even if it is good for eating plain rice or making sushi, Indica rice is more suitable for dishes such as curry. Therefore, I think rice should be chosen according to what kind of dish you are preparing.

I hear that there are about 560 diverse varieties of rice in Japan, and that around 260 of them are currently being grown. It is precisely because there are so many varieties that some people study how to produce delicious rice. In addition, not only rice but also rice-cooking utensils have been researched in many ways, so people can now cook extremely delicious rice.

Since Japanese cuisine became widely known, people in countries where bread was traditionally eaten have gradually begun eating rice as well. However, because rice itself has little flavor, some people say they cannot eat it unless they pour soy sauce over it. I never imagined that some people would eat the rice by itself and the side dishes by themselves. This may happen because they have only learned about the dishes themselves. Japanese side dishes taste perfectly balanced when eaten together with rice. If you eat the side dishes alone, they will taste too salty. Perhaps people even need to be taught how to eat rice properly.

（注1）和食：Japanese food

（注2）しょっぱい：Having a strong salty taste

default.p.55cong_n4-t34-p1.outline.1.note: It identifies problems caused by the excessive number of bicycles, including insufficient parking and accidents involving pedestrians, as well as the financial risk of riding without insurance. It argues that the government should make insurance mandatory.
default.p.55cong_n4-t34-p1.outline.2.label: The lack of bicycle lanes and a proposed solution
default.p.55cong_n4-t34-p1.outline.2.note: Based on the author's experience cycling the Shimanami Kaido, this passage describes Japan's shortage of dedicated bicycle lanes compared with other countries and expresses a desire to build more separate lanes for safety.
default.p.55cong_n4-t34-p1.outline.3.label: Vocabulary notes in the passage
default.p.55cong_n4-t34-p1.outline.3.note: Explains terms from the passage: 省エネ (energy conservation), ママチャリ (a basic city bicycle), 歩道 (sidewalk), and 保険 (accident insurance).
default.p.55cong_n4-t34-p1.vietnamese:
Bicycles are very convenient. In addition, although electric bicycles also exist, ordinary bicycles are powered by pedaling, so they do not consume fuel. Therefore, using a bicycle instead of a car saves energy. In Japan, many people ride mamachari. A mamachari does not require the rider to lift their legs high, so even people wearing skirts can ride one easily. I think mamachari have helped make bicycle use more widespread in Japan. Furthermore, while bicycles in many countries must travel in the same lanes as cars, in Japan bicycles are allowed on sidewalks for elderly people and children, as well as on sidewalks at least 3 meters wide or on dangerous roads, so people can travel with peace of mind.

Bicycles may seem to have nothing but advantages, but because there are so many of them, there are not enough bicycle parking spaces, and accidents are also occurring in which pedestrians are injured or killed. Although bicycle insurance is available, most people still have not enrolled. As a result, some people face difficulties after causing an accident and being required to pay substantial compensation. I think the government should make insurance enrollment mandatory, as it is for cars, before serious accidents occur.

A few days ago, I tried cycling the 70-kilometer route along the famous cycling road called the “Shimanami Kaido,” which is also popular with foreign tourists. I was concerned to see that most of the route consisted of ordinary roads and that there were very few dedicated bicycle paths. Compared with other countries, Japan has too few bicycle paths. To protect cyclists and pedestrians, I hope the authorities will build more roads exclusively for bicycles.

(Note 1) Saving energy: using less energy.

(Note 2) Mamachari: mama (mother) + chari (bicycle). A bicycle that is easy to get on and off and has a basket attached to the front for carrying things.

(Note 3) Sidewalk: a path for pedestrians.

(Note 4) Insurance: here, a service that pays costs incurred when someone causes an accident.

default.p.55cong_n4-t35-p1.outline.2.label: The true nature of “Hai” and “Iie” in Japanese
default.p.55cong_n4-t35-p1.outline.2.note: “Hai” means agreeing with the questioner’s statement—“That’s just as you said”—whereas “Iie” contradicts that statement.
default.p.55cong_n4-t35-p1.outline.3.label: Limitations of mechanical dictionary searches
default.p.55cong_n4-t35-p1.outline.3.note: A dictionary only provides equivalent words, which can lead to incorrect usage; rules for forms of address and real-life communication are also absent from dictionaries.
default.p.55cong_n4-t35-p1.outline.4.label: The importance of learning about culture and customs
default.p.55cong_n4-t35-p1.outline.4.note: States that using a language correctly requires not only a dictionary but also learning its culture and customs.
default.p.55cong_n4-t35-p1.vietnamese: An American once told me that it was strange for Japanese people to say「No, I like it」even when they liked something. He said that if they liked it, they should say「Yes」. This was because he thought that「いいえ (no)」meant the same thing as NO in English. For example, there is no problem when the answer to「a Is this apple delicious?」is「Yes, it is delicious」. However, when asked「b Isn’t this apple delicious?」, Japanese people may answer「Yes, it isn’t delicious」or「No, it is delicious」, which apparently confuses him. If a Japanese person says only「Yes」, he may mistakenly think that the apple is delicious. However, the Japanese word「Yes」means「That is as you say」, which is different from YES in English. Even if one says「Yes」, the apple is still not delicious. In Japanese,「Yes」and「No」are used to answer whether one agrees with what is being asked. In both (a) and (b),「Yes」is used when one means “That is correct,” and「No」when one means the opposite. However, because dictionaries list「Yes」as YES and「No」as NO, people never seem to learn to use them correctly. Similarly, because dictionaries say SHORT means short and BIG means large, people sometimes use strange Japanese such as「That person is a short person」or「I ate a big meal」. Dictionaries also do not mention such things as not calling an older person outside one’s family「You (Anata)」or not saying「Konnichiwa」to family members. Dictionaries are convenient, but they only provide meanings. I think it is difficult to use a language correctly without learning its culture and customs as well.

default.p.55cong_n4-t36-p1.outline.0.note: The passage lists numerous free services in Japan—drinking water, hand towels, no tipping, supermarket chopsticks, and wrapping—which have made Japanese people accustomed to thinking that services cost nothing.
default.p.55cong_n4-t36-p1.outline.1.label: The true cost of a free service
default.p.55cong_n4-t36-p1.outline.1.note: Affirms the unusually wide range of services available in Japan, but points out that the costs of supplies and labor are actually included in the prices paid by customers.
default.p.55cong_n4-t36-p1.outline.2.label: Unnecessary services that provide no real benefit
default.p.55cong_n4-t36-p1.outline.2.note: Transition: discusses services that are not truly necessary, such as wrapping gifts in many layers and providing personal items, which are costly and create additional troublesome waste.
default.p.55cong_n4-t36-p1.outline.3.label: The customer's attitude and the author's message
default.p.55cong_n4-t36-p1.outline.3.note: Criticizes some customers’ attitude that being served is only to be expected, and conveys the message that customers should always appreciate and respect service workers.
default.p.55cong_n4-t36-p1.vietnamese:
At Japanese restaurants, water or tea is usually brought out first. Many places also provide customers with a wet towel called an oshibori for wiping their hands. Hamburger restaurants often provide paper wet towels as well. These items are free of charge, so no payment is required. In Japan, even at expensive restaurants, customers do not need to tip the staff. Therefore, Japanese people tend to think of service as free (0 yen). When buying a boxed meal at a supermarket, an employee may ask, "How many pairs of chopsticks would you like?" and provide them free of charge. Nowadays, many stores require customers to pay for plastic bags, but until quite recently, every store provided them for free. Even when goods are beautifully wrapped, customers generally do not have to pay for the wrapping.

A country like this is quite rare. There probably is no other country with such a wide range of services as Japan. However, the supplies needed to provide these services, as well as workers' wages, are actually included in the prices of the goods and meals. We—the customers—are the ones paying that money.

Everyone is happy and feels comfortable when they receive attentive service. However, some services are unnecessary. Items for home use can simply be taken home as they are. Even gifts do not need to be wrapped in layer after layer. Wrapping paper becomes trash and can sometimes be a nuisance.

Furthermore, customers may think that being served by employees is only natural. Because they think only of themselves, they may get angry and complain that an employee is serving them too slowly. When I see people like that, I feel sorry for the employees who are always working so hard. For the service they receive, I hope customers will always show gratitude and say, "Thank you."

(Note) ただ: 0 yen

default.p.55cong_n4-t37-p1.vietnamese:
There is a Japanese proverb: “When there is laughter, good fortune comes” (when a home is filled with laughter, good luck will come). It means that “when a home is always filled with laughter, good things will come.” People's ways of thinking are not all that different, so although the wording may vary, other countries surely have similar proverbs.

When we laugh, our physical health improves. This is because the immune system becomes stronger and the body can relax. Therefore, in everyday life, it is good to have cheerful conversations with someone or watch entertaining television programs. However, there are also times when we feel sad or suffer. Even at such times, it is said that deliberately making a smiling face can make us feel better in the same way. Perhaps we do not laugh because we are happy; rather, laughing makes us feel happy. If you put something such as a chopstick between your teeth, you can easily create a smile, so why not give it a try?

Moreover, it is said to be even better if you laugh out loud. People say that when we laugh aloud, many parts of the body move vigorously, which is very beneficial. When researchers investigated whether men or women laugh aloud more, the results showed that 40% of men and 60% of women laughed aloud. So perhaps that is one reason women live longer. Children also laugh often, but as people grow older, they seem to laugh less and less. This may be due to stress. It seems that the more we laugh, the more healthily and happily we can live. Laughing does not cost any money. I think there is no method this wonderful.

(Note 1) Proverb: Something handed down from long ago, expressing a lesson. A short sentence made easy to say and remember.

(Note 2) Immunity: The body's ability to prevent illness or heal disease.

(Note 3) Hold in the mouth: To bite or keep something between the upper and lower teeth.

default.p.55cong_n4-t38-p1.vietnamese:
Japan’s population is declining, and there is a shortage of workers. Some people say that everything will be fine if more elderly people and women work. However, because working conditions are unsuitable and facilities such as day-care centers, which people with young children need in order to work, are also in short supply, some people cannot work even though they want to. Japan today is not a society where it is easy to work.

At present, the people working in place of Japanese workers are foreigners. Some are married to Japanese people or are descendants of people of Japanese origin, but most are international students and technical interns. International students who are allowed to work 28 hours a week often work at convenience stores, boxed-meal factories, pubs, or in cleaning. Many technical interns work in agriculture, fishing, and manufacturing. Technical interns come to Japan to learn skills, yet they are forced to work for extremely low wages. Many have borrowed money to come to Japan, and because they cannot change jobs, they cannot quit even when working conditions are terrible. Some become ill or injured, and some even die. This problem must be solved quickly in some way. That is both for their sake and for ours. If some people work under terrible conditions, the working conditions of others cannot improve either.

In 2018, a law was enacted allowing more foreigners to work in Japan. It is said that half of the technical interns will switch to working under this law. Will this lead to more foreigners coming to work in Japan? If Japan remains a country where it is as difficult to work as it is now, foreigners may not choose Japan.

(Note 1) Working conditions: working hours, days off, wages received, etc.

(Note 2) Day-care center: a place that cares for children and supports families.

(Note 3) Descendants of people of Japanese origin: children of people who were once Japanese, or the children of those children.

(Note 4) Technical intern: a person who comes to Japan to learn Japanese skills and techniques.

(Note 5) Agriculture, fishing, and manufacturing: agriculture involves producing rice, vegetables, and so on; fishing involves work related to fish; manufacturing involves making goods.

(Note 6) Law: a rule established by a country or government.

(☆) Specified Skilled Worker: since 2019, foreigners have begun working under the law concerning “Specified Skilled Workers,” which permits employment in fields such as elderly care, factories, and stores.

default.p.55cong_n4-t39-p1.vietnamese:
Japan has many long-established businesses. “Shinise” refers to shops or companies that have continued operating for a long time. According to one statistic, there are 5,586 businesses worldwide that have existed for more than 200 years, and more than half of them—3,146 businesses—are reportedly in Japan. Germany has 837, the Netherlands 222, and France 196. The world’s oldest business is also said to have been founded in Japan in 578. Japan apparently has 7 businesses that are more than 1,000 years old, 32 that are more than 500 years old, 3,146 that are more than 200 years old, and as many as 50,000 that are more than 100 years old. However, 89.4% of these businesses are small businesses with fewer than 300 employees. The reasons there are so many long-established businesses are said to be: (1) wars are relatively rare in Japan, (2) businesses place importance on their core lines of business, and (3) businesses take a long-term view. All of these reasons are obvious. In particular, when we consider how many companies abandoned their main lines of business during the economic bubble and instead bought and sold land and buildings, only to close down or fall into difficulty afterward, the importance of a core business becomes clear.

Valuing one’s core business does not mean continuing to do exactly the same thing forever. Businesses survive for a long time by adapting to each era and continually improving their main lines of business. GE, founded by Edison in 1892, still exists today because it has constantly changed to keep up with the times. Only businesses that both value their core business and continually take on new challenges can survive for more than 100 years. Once any long-established business stops taking on challenges, it will certainly come to an end at that point.

(Note 1) Business: Here, this refers to a shop or company.

(Note 2) Core business: The main work or business activity.

(Note 3) Long-term vision: Thinking ahead about long-term issues.

(Note 4) Bubble period: The period from late 1986 to early 1991, when the economy was extremely prosperous.

Look at the notice about the Citizens’ Festival on the next page, then answer the questions below. Choose the best answer from 1, 2, 3, and 4.

About the Citizens’ Festival

1. Date and time: October 9 (Saturday) and 10 (Sunday), from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

2. Participants (Note 1): Nonprofit organizations (Note 2) of citizens of Nishi City

・Performances (Note 3): Participation fee: 10,000 yen. Singing, dancing, magic, and other groups may participate. There is no age limit.

Look at the information about the supplementary classes on the next page and answer the questions below. For each answer, choose the best answer from 1, 2, 3, and 4.

Free supplementary classes (Note 1) for elementary and junior high school students.

We offer free lessons to elementary and junior high school students who cannot afford to attend a cram school (Note 2) or receive tutoring (Note 3).

Eligibility:

Eligible students range from those newly entering fifth grade of elementary school to those newly entering eighth grade (second year of junior high school). However, current eighth-grade students who are already attending the classes and wish to continue may also apply. Current students should submit their application forms to their teacher in class. First-time applicants must attend an information session.

Classes: Japanese language (3 classes), arithmetic (3 classes), mathematics (3 classes), English (3 classes)

Each person may attend two classes. Write your name, date of birth, school name, grade, address, telephone number, and the days and times of the classes you wish to take on the application form and submit it. If many people want to join the same class, the class teachers will discuss the matter and decide, so it is not yet certain which class you will be assigned to. Number the classes you wish to join from 1 to 6. In some cases, you may be able to attend only one class.

Orientation / information sessions:

① Time: Saturday, February 27, and Sunday, February 28, at 10:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. (lasting one hour). Attend one of the four sessions. Please try to come with a parent or another family member. After hearing about your family circumstances and your reasons for wanting to participate, we will decide on the class and contact you.

② Location: Meeting Room, 2nd floor, City Hall (Shimin Kaikan)

(Note 1) Free: 0 yen.

(Note 2) Cram school: a place that is not a regular school but provides instruction to students.

(Note 3) Tutor: a person who teaches at home or a similar location.

Please read the notice about the volleyball tournament and the request to teachers on the following page, then answer the questions below. For each answer, choose the most appropriate option from 1, 2, 3, and 4.

Notice about the Volleyball Tournament

Date: December 20 (Friday)

Morning session: 9:30 to 12:00. Please assemble by 9:15.

Afternoon session: 1:00 to 3:30. Please assemble by 12:45.

Location: West Gymnasium (Note 1), a 5-minute walk from Midorigaoka Station.

Teachers will be standing at the station and at turns along the route to show you the way.

Clothing: Comfortable clothing that allows easy movement. You must bring indoor shoes (Note 2). If you forget them, you will have to play barefoot (Note 3), so be careful not to leave them behind.

Other: There will also be gifts.

Assembly times: Morning-session teachers: 9:00

Afternoon-session teachers: 12:30

Duties: Morning-session teachers: Prepare from 9:00. Check students' attendance at the reception desk (Note 5).

Afternoon-session teachers: Check students' attendance at the reception desk. Clean up after the matches.

Present the prizes and gifts after the morning and afternoon matches.

Other: Please briefly explain the 「Volleyball Tournament」 in class before the event.

(Note 2) Indoor shoes: Here, shoes to be worn inside the gymnasium.

(Note 3) Barefoot: The state of wearing nothing on one's feet.

(Note 4) Prize: An item given to honor a good achievement.

(Note 5) Check attendance: Check whether someone is present or absent.

Apparently, because the number of tourists has increased, it has become impossible to book hotel rooms. As a result, some foreigners choose to stay in private homes. default.p.55cong_n4-t50-p1.vietnamese:
About the Children’s Goods Exchange Club

・Giving away and exchanging children’s goods with one another.

① Clothes, shoes, hats, toys, CDs, DVDs, etc. Write the necessary information on a pink「giveaway form」at the reception desk, and submit it to the reception desk together with the item.

② For large items such as strollers, bicycles, and beds, take a photograph. Write the name of the item on a light-blue「giveaway form」and submit it to the reception desk together with the photograph. The photograph will be posted beside the reception desk.

③ If there is an item you would like to give away or receive, write the name of the item on a yellow「giveaway form」at the reception desk and register. Only the name of the item will be posted. Those wishing to give away an item should contact the reception desk.

Notes:

１．On the「giveaway form」, write the item’s name, your full name, address, telephone number, etc.

２．Only items that can be used immediately in their current condition may be given away. Dirty items or items requiring repairs cannot be accepted. Up to 5 items may be given away at one time.

３．Selling items is not permitted.

４．Items will be posted for 3 months. If no one claims an item after 3 months, take it home.

５．The recipient must arrange transportation of the item.

６．Both the giver and the recipient should fill out and register using「forms」of the same color.

(Note 1) ゆずる／ゆずり合う：ゆずる means to give or hand over.
ゆずり合う means to give and receive from one another.

(Note 2) 掲示する：To write information to be announced on paper and put it up

default.p.55cong_n4-t51-p1.vietnamese:
Sumida River Boat Excursion

This is an experiential tour of Japan accompanied by a guide.

Itinerary:

① Hama-rikyu Gardens: Have tea in a tea room (Note 1) and admire the Japanese-style garden.

② Boat ride: Travel upstream on the Sumida River by boat for approximately 50 minutes, from Hama-rikyu to Asakusa. Enjoy the cherry blossoms along the Sumida River. The area near Asakusa is especially full of cherry trees and is truly spectacular.

③ Asakusa: After visiting Sensoji Temple, enjoy a meal at a Japanese restaurant.

Cost: 9,800 yen per adult, including admission to Hama-rikyu Gardens, the boat ride, and lunch.

Dates: Every day from March 21 to April 8

Meeting time: 9:30 a.m.

Meeting place: East Exit of Shiodome Station on the Oedo Line

Number of participants (Note 2): Up to 20 people (the tour will be canceled if fewer than 10 people register)

Reservations: Call 03-333-××××. Reservations can also be made through the website.

Note: There may be times when few cherry blossoms can be seen. The tour will take place regardless of the weather.

(Note 1) Tea room: A place where the tea ceremony is conducted

(Note 2) Participant: A person who does something together with others. Here, it means a person who has registered for this tour

default.p.55cong_n4-t54-p1.vietnamese:
Look at the instructions for making 「Simple Tofu Dish」 on the next page and answer the questions below. For each answer, choose the most appropriate one from 1, 2, 3, and 4.

Simple Tofu Dish

Ingredients
Mixed ground meat (Note 1): 150 g
If unavailable, use beef or pork
Onion: half a medium-sized onion
Ketchup: 5 tablespoons
Sauce: 5 tablespoons
Salt: a little
Pepper: a little
Tofu: 1 block
Melting cheese (Note 2):
100 g ~ 150 g
Powdered cheese: a little, if available

① Cut the tofu into cubes approximately 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm, then briefly boil it first. If you do not boil it beforehand, it will take much longer later.

② Finely chop the onion (Note 4).

③ Put the onion, meat, ketchup, and sauce into a frying pan and simmer over low heat for 3–4 minutes (Note 5).

④ After step ③ is complete, add the salt and pepper and mix well (Note 6), then turn off the heat. The meat sauce is now finished.
You can also use ready-made meat sauce.

⑤ Put the tofu in a heatproof dish (Note 7), cover it with the meat sauce, and place the melting cheese on top.

⑥ Finally, sprinkling powdered cheese on top will make it even tastier.

⑦ Heat it in an oven or microwave until the cheese melts. It will be even tastier if the cheese is browned in an oven.

※ Eggplant can also be used instead of tofu and tastes delicious. I think you should try making it in various ways.

(Note 1) Mixed ground meat: Meat made by finely chopping beef and pork and mixing them together. If it is not sold, mince the meat yourself to make it.

(Note 2) Melting cheese: A type of cheese that softens when exposed to high temperatures.

(Note 3) Boil: Heat something in boiling water without adding seasoning.

(Note 4) Finely chop: Cut something into very small pieces.

(Note 5) Cook/simmer: Put ingredients together with salt, sugar, and so on in water, then turn on the heat. Leave the heat on until the ingredients become soft.

(Note 6) Mix/stir: Combine two or more things together.

(Note 7) Heatproof: The property of an object remaining safe when heated by fire or heat.

default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) したい
The desire form 「〜たい」 combines with the causal conjunction 「ので」 to form 「したいので」 (“because they want to do it”), explaining why the children and teacher decided to hold a farewell party.
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q1.explanation: The sentence containing the blank is: 「それで子供たちがお別れ会を（ したい ）のですることにしました。」 Grammatically, the verb 「する」is changed into the desiderative form 「したい」(remove ます from the ます-form and add たい). It functions like an i-adjective and connects directly to the reason conjunction 「ので」, forming 「したいので」. The complete sentence means: "Therefore, since the children wanted to hold a farewell party, we decided to hold one." A common source of confusion is the belief that the third-person subject 「子供たち」must use 「したがった」. However, 「〜たがる」is used when observing another person's outward behavior or appearance, whereas when presenting someone's desire as an objective reason leading to a subsequent action, Japanese commonly uses the plain form 「たいので」. Also distinguish 「ほしい」(want to have an object, used with が) from 「たい」(want to perform an action, used with を, as in 「お別れ会をしたい」).
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) 「するはずな」expresses a confident expectation, which logically conflicts with using it as the reason for just deciding 「することにしました」.
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) 「ほしい」expresses the desire to possess a noun marked by 「が」. It cannot combine directly with the object phrase 「お別れ会を」.
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) 「したがった」 is generally used to describe another person's outward signs or apparent desire, so it is unnatural before 「ので」 when stating the reason for a shared decision.
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q1.why.3: ✓ (d) 「したい」 correctly combines with 「ので」 to form 「したいので」, expressing the children’s wish and leading to the decision 「することにしました」.
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 8個入りを2箱とばらで4個
A total of 20 cakes is needed for 18 students and 2 teachers. Option (c) minimizes the cost, with the lowest price of 1,800 yen.
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q2.explanation: The passage states 「今学童保育所（注1）に子供が18人と先生が2人います。」 and 「ケーキはばら（注2）で買うと1つ100円ですが、8個入りの箱は700円で、6個入りの箱は550円です。」 There are 20 people in total—18 children and 2 teachers—so 20 cakes are needed. Individual cakes cost 100 yen each; boxes of 8 cost 700 yen, and boxes of 6 cost 550 yen. The grammar is 「V-る + つもりです」, using the dictionary form to express a future intention or plan. The key word 「ばら」 in 「ばらで」 means buying individual units rather than boxed items. To minimize the cost, buy two boxes of 8 (16 cakes for 1,400 yen) and four individual cakes (400 yen), for an optimal total of 1,800 yen. Do not be distracted by 「3月に5人のお友だちがやめる予定です」 and subtract five children; calculate the cost based on the current total of 20 people.
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q2.why.0: ✗ (a) Buying all 20 cakes individually costs 2,000 yen (20 × 100 yen), making it the most expensive option.
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) Buying 3 boxes of 6 items and 2 individual items costs 1,850 yen (3 × 550 + 2 × 100), which is more expensive than option c.
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q2.why.2: ✓ (c) Buying two boxes of eight and four individual items gives exactly 20 items at the lowest cost: 1,800 yen (2 × 700 + 4 × 100).
default.q.55cong_n4-t1-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) Buying two boxes of 8 pieces and one box of 6 pieces gives 22 pieces for a total of 1,950 yen (2 × 700 + 550), which is more expensive than option c.
default.q.55cong_n4-t10-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) なら
Among the conditional forms, only 「なら」can follow a noun directly to make that time the condition.
default.q.55cong_n4-t10-q1.explanation: Based on the sentence from the passage: 「5日、15日、25日（　　）2倍のポイントがもらえる。」, the words before the blank are nouns indicating dates: 「5日、15日、25日」. Grammatically, the pattern 「N + なら」uses a noun to present a hypothetical condition or limit the scope of a time period, with the sense of "if it is" or "in the case of". It is therefore suitable for specifying when the special offer applies. With 「なら」inserted, the complete sentence means: "On the 5th, 15th, and 25th, you will receive double the points." For N4 conditional expressions 「と・ば・たら・なら」, remember that only 「なら」can follow a noun directly. 「と」requires 「だと」, 「ば」requires 「であれば」, and 「たら」requires the past form 「だったら」.
default.q.55cong_n4-t10-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) 「と」 combines with the dictionary form of a verb, or requires 「だ」 when used with a noun; it cannot be attached directly after a noun.
default.q.55cong_n4-t10-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) 「ば」 is the conditional form of a verb or adjective. With a noun, it must be changed to 「であれば」.
default.q.55cong_n4-t10-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) 「たら」must follow the past form. When it is used with a noun, the noun must be changed to 「だったら」.
default.q.55cong_n4-t10-q1.why.3: ✓ (d) 「なら」 can directly follow a noun (N + なら), meaning “if it is...” or “as for...,” so it is appropriate both grammatically and contextually.
default.q.55cong_n4-t10-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 2000円
Ali used all 500 points available on the card to deduct from the 2,500-yen purchase total the next day, so the actual amount payable was 2,000 yen.
default.q.55cong_n4-t10-q2.explanation: The passage uses the key N4 pattern `V-た ほうがいい`, in which a verb in the past form `た` is followed by `ほうがいい`. It gives advice or suggests that an action would be better in a particular situation; here, a staff member advises Ali to save the points for another day. The passage as a whole means: "At a supermarket near his home, customers receive 1 point for every 100 yen they spend; 1 point is worth 1 yen; on the 5th, 15th, and 25th of each month, customers receive double points. On the 15th, Ali went shopping with a card containing 500 points and spent 3,000 yen, but because a staff member advised him that it would be better to use the points on another day, he did not use them. The next day, when he spent 2,500 yen, he used all the points." The answer is supported by 「500ポイントあるカードを持って買い物に行った」 and 「次の日2500円の買い物をした時にポイントを全部使った」, showing that Ali used the 500 points already on his card, equivalent to deducting 500 yen from the next day's 2,500-yen bill. Do not incorrectly choose (b) 1970円 or (c) 1940円 by assuming that points earned on the 15th should be added; the passage only confirms that Ali had and used the original 500 points.
default.q.55cong_n4-t10-q2.why.0: ✓ (a) Correct, because Ali must pay the price of the item, 2,500 yen, minus all 500 points available on the card (2,500 − 500 = 2,000 yen).

The key grammar is 「plain form + し」, an N4 pattern used to list features or reasons with the meaning “both... and...” or “not only... but also...”. It combines with the potential-form verb 「遊べる」 (“can play”) to describe experiences the park offers. However, 「～て」 connects actions in sequence, while 「～たり」 must be followed by 「する」 at the end of the clause. The pattern 「V-る / V-ない + こと」 attaches directly to the dictionary form or short negative form (nai-form) and expresses a formal, objective instruction or indirect command. It is commonly used in notices, regulations, and examination questions to mean “must do...” or “must not do....” The completed passage means: “Guesthouse Rules: 1. Do not smoke inside the house. 2.
